chapters.n: Paul opens his letter to the Corinthian saints the way ancient letters began — with the sender’s name. He reminds them that his apostleship came from God’s will, not his own ambition, and includes Sosthenes, a fellow believer.

f.g: Greek apostolos — one who is sent out with authority as a messenger.

chapters.n: The letter is addressed to the Church in Corinth, a wealthy, worldly port city in Greece. Paul calls them people made holy through Christ and called to be saints — together with believers everywhere.

f.g: A large Roman colony and trading center in southern Greece, known for wealth and loose morals.
Made holy, set apart for God.

chapters.n: Paul’s standard blessing joins the Greek greeting (grace) and the Hebrew greeting (peace), both flowing from the Father and the Son.

f.w: Grace be unto you, and peace

chapters.n: Though Paul will correct the Corinthians sharply, he starts with sincere gratitude for the grace God has given them through Jesus Christ.

f.g: God’s freely given help, favor, and enabling power through Christ.

chapters.n: Christ has made them rich in spiritual gifts — especially in speaking and in knowledge, two areas the Corinthians prized highly (and sometimes misused).

f.g: Speech — the ability to express spiritual truth, including gifts like tongues and prophecy.

chapters.n: These gifts were evidence that the testimony of Christ Paul preached had taken root among them and been confirmed by the Spirit.
They lacked no spiritual gift while they waited for the Second Coming. Early saints lived with eager expectation of the Lord’s return.

f.g: Fall short in no gift; lack nothing.

chapters.n: Christ will keep them strong to the end so they can stand blameless at his coming — a promise that rests on his power, not their perfection.

f.w: the day of our Lord Jesus Christ
f.g: The day of His Second Coming and judgment.

chapters.n: God keeps His promises. He invited them into fellowship — a shared life and partnership — with His Son.

f.g: Greek koinonia — sharing, communion, partnership.

chapters.n: Now Paul turns to the main problem: division. He pleads with them to be unified — to speak with one voice and share one mind and purpose, like a torn net mended back together.

f.g: Greek katartizo — to mend or restore, as fishermen repaired nets.

chapters.n: Members of Chloe’s household — perhaps her servants or family traveling on business — had reported to Paul that the Corinthian saints were quarreling.
The saints had formed fan clubs around leaders: some followed Paul, some Apollos, some Peter, and some proudly claimed only Christ. Rivalry had replaced unity.

f.g: An eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria who taught in Corinth after Paul.
The Aramaic name of Peter, meaning “rock.”

chapters.n: Paul’s sharp questions expose the absurdity: Christ cannot be split into pieces. Paul was not crucified for them, and they were not baptized into Paul’s name but Christ’s.
Given the factions, Paul is glad he personally baptized very few of them — Crispus, the former synagogue ruler, and Gaius.
That way no one could claim they belonged to Paul because he baptized them. Baptism binds us to Christ, not to the person who performs it.
Paul corrects himself: he also baptized Stephanas’s household. Beyond that he can’t recall — the point is that who baptized whom doesn’t matter.
Paul’s main assignment was to preach, not to perform baptisms himself. He deliberately avoided impressive rhetoric so that the power of Christ’s cross, not his eloquence, would convert people.

f.g: Clever, polished speech — the trained rhetoric Greeks admired.
Emptied of its power.

chapters.n: To those headed for destruction, a message about a crucified Savior sounds foolish. To those being saved, it is God’s very power.
Paul quotes Isaiah: God promised to overturn the self-assured wisdom of the worldly wise.

f.w: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise

chapters.n: Where are the philosophers, the legal scholars, and the clever debaters now? God has shown that the world’s wisdom cannot save.

f.g: A Jewish expert in the law of Moses.
A debater or philosopher who argues points for sport.

chapters.n: In God’s wise plan, human cleverness could never find God on its own. So He chose to save believers through preaching that the world calls foolish.

f.g: The seemingly foolish message preached — Christ crucified — not foolish preaching style.

chapters.n: Paul’s Jewish listeners wanted miraculous proof; his Greek listeners wanted impressive philosophy. Each audience had its own demand.
But Paul preaches a crucified Messiah. To Jews, a Messiah hung on a cross was offensive; to Greeks, worshiping an executed man seemed ridiculous.

f.g: Greek skandalon — something that trips people up or offends.

chapters.n: But for those who answer God’s call, whatever their background, Christ is both the power of God the Jews sought and the wisdom of God the Greeks sought.
Even what looks like foolishness or weakness in God surpasses humanity’s greatest wisdom and strength. Paul uses irony to make the point.

f.w: the weakness of God is stronger than men

chapters.n: Paul invites them to look at their own congregation: not many were educated, powerful, or from noble families by worldly standards.

f.g: By human, worldly standards.

chapters.n: God deliberately chose the humble and weak to shame those who think themselves wise and strong. His work doesn’t depend on worldly status.

f.w: the weak things of the world

chapters.n: He even chose the lowly, the despised, and the “nobodies” to bring to nothing what the world considers important.

f.g: Lowly things, of low birth or status.
People counted as nothing in society.

chapters.n: The purpose: no human being can boast before God. Salvation is His gift, not our achievement.

f.g: Here, to boast or brag.

chapters.n: It is God who placed them in Christ, and Christ becomes everything they need: true wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption.

f.g: Release purchased by a price — like freeing a slave or prisoner.

chapters.n: Paul quotes Jeremiah: if anyone wants to boast, let them boast about the Lord and what He has done.

f.w: He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord

chapters.n: When Paul first came to Corinth, he did not try to impress with polished speeches or philosophy. He simply bore witness of what God had done.

f.g: Superior, showy eloquence.

chapters.n: Paul resolved to focus on one thing only: Jesus Christ and His crucifixion. The Atonement was the center of his message.
Paul admits he arrived feeling weak, anxious, and shaken — possibly after rough experiences in Philippi, Thessalonica, and Athens. God’s power worked through his weakness.
His preaching didn’t rely on persuasive techniques. Instead, the Holy Ghost confirmed his words with real spiritual power.
Paul wanted their faith grounded on God’s power, not on clever arguments. Faith built on human cleverness can be knocked down by a cleverer argument.
Paul does teach wisdom — to the spiritually mature. But it is not the wisdom of the age or its rulers, whose power is already passing away.

f.g: Mature, complete, spiritually grown-up.
The rulers of this age, both human and possibly spiritual powers.

chapters.n: This is God’s wisdom, once hidden and now revealed — a plan He set up before the world was created for His children’s glory.

f.g: A truth known only by revelation.

chapters.n: The world’s rulers did not understand God’s plan; if they had, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.
Paul paraphrases Isaiah: no human eye, ear, or imagination can fully grasp what God has prepared for those who love Him.
Yet these things are not completely unknowable — God reveals them by His Spirit, who searches out even the deepest truths of God.

f.w: revealed them unto us by his Spirit

chapters.n: Just as only a person’s own spirit knows his inner thoughts, only God’s Spirit knows the things of God. JST says “except he has the Spirit of God.”

f.w: the things of God knoweth no man
f.g: JST: “the things of God knoweth no man, except he has the Spirit of God.”

chapters.n: The saints have received God’s Spirit, not the spirit of the world, so they can understand the gifts God freely gives them.
Paul teaches these truths in words the Holy Ghost provides, explaining spiritual truths to spiritual people.

f.g: Or: explaining spiritual truths in spiritual words.

chapters.n: The “natural man” — a person living only by fallen, earthly instincts — rejects spiritual things as nonsense, because they can only be understood through the Spirit.

f.g: Judged and understood by spiritual means.

chapters.n: A spiritual person can evaluate all things rightly, but the world cannot properly judge him, because it lacks the Spirit.

f.g: Discerns, examines, evaluates.

chapters.n: Quoting Isaiah, Paul asks who could ever instruct the Lord. Yet through the Spirit, believers can share the very mind of Christ.

f.w: who hath known the mind of the Lord

chapters.n: Paul couldn’t teach the Corinthians deep spiritual things because they were still acting worldly — like spiritual infants in Christ.

f.g: Fleshly; ruled by worldly, natural impulses.

chapters.n: Like a parent with a baby, Paul gave them milk (basic teachings) instead of solid food. Even now they aren’t ready for more.
Their jealousy and quarreling prove they are still immature — behaving like ordinary people without the Spirit.
Lining up behind favorite leaders is itself evidence of worldliness.
Paul and Apollos are only servants — instruments through whom the Corinthians came to believe, each doing the job the Lord gave him.

f.g: Servants (Greek diakonoi), not masters.

chapters.n: Paul uses a farming picture: he planted the seed of the gospel in Corinth, Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.
Neither the planter nor the waterer deserves the credit. Growth comes from God alone.

f.w: neither is he that planteth any thing
f.g: The planter counts for nothing by comparison.

chapters.n: Paul and Apollos are on the same team with the same goal. Each will be rewarded for his own faithful work.
The workers labor alongside God. The saints themselves are God’s farm field and God’s building — the place where He works.

f.g: A cultivated field or farm.

chapters.n: Shifting to a building image, Paul says he laid the foundation in Corinth as a skilled master builder. Others now build on it, and they must build carefully.

f.g: Greek architekton — chief builder, architect.

chapters.n: The only true foundation is Jesus Christ. Any life or church built on another foundation will not stand.
On that foundation people build with materials of very different quality — some lasting and precious, some cheap and flammable.

f.w: gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble
f.g: Contrasting durable, valuable materials with ones that burn easily.

chapters.n: Each person’s work will be revealed on the day of judgment, which will test it like fire tests building materials.
If what someone built survives the test, he will be rewarded.
If someone’s work burns up, he loses that reward — though he himself may still be saved, like a person escaping a burning house.

f.g: Like someone barely rescued through flames.

chapters.n: The Corinthian congregation together is God’s temple, a holy place where His Spirit lives. Later Paul applies this to each body as well.

f.w: ye are the temple of God

chapters.n: Anyone who damages God’s temple — by division or by sin — will answer to God, because that temple is sacred.

f.g: Corrupt, ruin, destroy.

chapters.n: Paul warns against self-deception. Anyone who thinks he is wise by worldly standards should become “foolish” in the world’s eyes so he can gain true wisdom.
God sees the world’s wisdom as foolishness. Paul quotes Job: God catches the clever in their own scheming.

f.w: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness

chapters.n: Quoting a psalm, Paul adds that the Lord knows the reasoning of the wise is empty.

f.w: The Lord knoweth the thoughts of the wise

f.g: Empty, useless.

chapters.n: So stop boasting about human leaders. Instead of belonging to Paul or Apollos, the saints should realize everything belongs to them.
Leaders, the world, life, death, the present, the future — all serve the saints’ good. They don’t belong to leaders; leaders belong to them.
The saints belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to the Father. That is the true order — not loyalty to rival teachers.
Paul asks the saints to see their leaders correctly: as servants of Christ and as stewards entrusted with God’s revealed truths — not as celebrities.

f.g: Household managers who care for a master’s property, accountable to him.

chapters.n: The one thing required of a steward is faithfulness to the master who appointed him.
Paul isn’t worried about how the Corinthians or any human court rates him. He doesn’t even make himself the final judge of his own service.

f.g: Literally “man’s day” — a human court’s verdict, in contrast to the Lord’s day of judgment.

chapters.n: Paul’s conscience is clear, but that doesn’t prove he is innocent. Only the Lord’s judgment counts.

f.g: I am not aware of any wrongdoing on my part.

chapters.n: So don’t pass final judgment on anyone before the Lord comes. He will bring hidden things to light and reveal people’s motives, and each faithful person will receive praise from God.

f.g: Hidden intentions and motives.

chapters.n: Paul used himself and Apollos as an example so the saints would learn not to go beyond what scripture teaches and not to puff themselves up by favoring one leader over another.

f.g: Applied as an illustration.
Inflated with pride, like a bellows.

chapters.n: Paul deflates their pride: who made you special? Every gift you have was given to you. Why brag as if you earned it?

f.w: what hast thou that thou didst not receive?

chapters.n: With biting irony Paul says: You think you’ve already arrived — full, rich, ruling like kings — without us! I wish you really did reign, so we could share it.

f.g: Some Corinthians seemed to think they had already reached full spiritual glory.

chapters.n: Meanwhile the apostles are treated like condemned prisoners paraded last in a Roman victory march or arena, a spectacle for the world, angels, and people to stare at.

f.g: Greek theatron — a show in a theater or arena.

chapters.n: More irony: the apostles are fools, weak, and despised for Christ, while the Corinthians imagine themselves wise, strong, and honored.
Paul describes his real life as a missionary: hungry, thirsty, poorly clothed, beaten, and homeless.

f.g: Struck with fists, roughly treated.

chapters.n: He worked with his own hands to support himself. When insulted, he blessed; when persecuted, he endured — just as Jesus taught.
When slandered, they answered kindly. The world treated them like garbage, the scrapings everyone throws out.

f.g: Dirt scraped off; the lowest scum.
Speak gently, appeal kindly.

chapters.n: Paul’s tone softens. He isn’t trying to humiliate them; he warns them as a loving father warns his children.
They might have countless tutors in the faith, but only one spiritual father — Paul, who brought them to Christ through the gospel.

f.g: Greek paidagogos — a guardian who escorted children; a tutor, not a parent.

chapters.n: So he urges them to follow his example of humble discipleship.
That’s why Paul sent Timothy, his faithful “son” in the gospel, to remind them of Paul’s Christlike way of life — the same thing he teaches in every church.
Some arrogant members were acting as if Paul would never come back to hold them accountable.
Paul plans to come soon, God willing, and he will test not their talk but their actual spiritual power.
God’s kingdom isn’t a matter of impressive words but of real power — changed lives and the Spirit at work.

f.w: not in word, but in power

chapters.n: Paul gives them a choice: should he come with a rod of discipline, or with love and gentleness? Their repentance will decide.

f.g: A symbol of fatherly correction.

chapters.n: Paul turns to a shocking report: a member was living in a sexual relationship with his stepmother — something even the pagan world considered scandalous.

f.g: Greek porneia — any sexual immorality.

chapters.n: Instead of grieving and removing the man from fellowship, the congregation was proud — perhaps of their supposed tolerance.

f.g: Grieved as over a death.

chapters.n: Though Paul is far away, he is with them in spirit and has already reached a judgment about the man.

f.w: absent in body, but present in spirit

chapters.n: He instructs them to act formally, gathered in Christ’s name and with His authority, with Paul united with them in spirit.

f.w: In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ

chapters.n: The man is to be excommunicated — handed over to Satan’s territory outside the Church — so that his sinful nature may be broken and his spirit ultimately saved. Church discipline aims at redemption.

f.w: deliver such an one unto Satan
f.g: Expel him from the Church’s protection and fellowship.

f.w: that the spirit may be saved

chapters.n: Their boasting is wrong. Just as a pinch of yeast spreads through a whole batch of dough, tolerated sin spreads through a whole community.

f.w: a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump

f.g: Yeast or sourdough starter; often a symbol of corruption.

chapters.n: At Passover, Jews cleared every bit of yeast from their homes. Christ is our Passover Lamb, already sacrificed, so the saints should clear sin from their lives.

f.g: Without yeast, like Passover bread.

chapters.n: So let us celebrate the true feast — not with old sin, malice, and wickedness, but with the pure bread of sincerity and truth.
Paul mentions an earlier letter (now lost) in which he told them not to associate with sexually immoral people.

f.g: A previous letter to Corinth that has not survived.

chapters.n: He didn’t mean to avoid all immoral or greedy people outside the Church — that would require leaving the world entirely.

f.g: Swindlers, people who take by force or fraud.

chapters.n: He meant they shouldn’t keep close fellowship with a professing member who persists in serious sin — not even sharing a meal that signals full approval.

f.g: A verbal abuser, someone who insults and slanders.
Someone claiming to be a Church member.

chapters.n: Church discipline isn’t for outsiders. Paul’s and the Church’s responsibility is to judge within the community of members.

f.g: Those outside the Church.

chapters.n: God will judge outsiders. The Corinthians must remove the unrepentant sinner from among them, echoing a phrase from Deuteronomy.

f.w: put away from among yourselves that wicked person

chapters.n: Paul is appalled that members were suing one another in pagan courts instead of settling disputes within the Church.

f.g: Take someone to court.
Here, unbelieving judges outside the Church.

chapters.n: The saints will one day help judge the world. Surely they can handle small disputes among themselves!

f.w: the saints shall judge the world

chapters.n: They will even judge angels — likely fallen angels. How much more can they handle everyday matters?
So if they have ordinary disputes, why hand them to people the Church doesn’t esteem? Many read this as a question rather than a command.

f.g: Those of no standing in the Church — likely the outside judges.

chapters.n: Paul says this to shame them: is there really no one wise enough in the congregation to settle a disagreement between members?
Instead, brother sues brother — in front of unbelievers, damaging the Church’s witness.

f.g: Exposing internal quarrels to outsiders.

chapters.n: Having lawsuits at all is already a defeat. Why not rather accept a wrong or a loss than fight your brother in court?
Worse, some of them were the ones doing wrong and cheating their own brothers and sisters in the faith.

f.g: Cheat, rob.

chapters.n: Paul reminds them that the unrighteous won’t inherit God’s kingdom, then lists sins that exclude people, including sexual sins and idolatry.

f.w: effeminate, nor abusers of themselves with mankind
f.g: Greek terms generally understood to refer to men taking part in homosexual acts.

chapters.n: The list continues: thieves, the greedy, drunkards, verbal abusers, and swindlers will not inherit God’s kingdom unless they repent.

f.g: Those who insult and abuse with words.

f.w: shall inherit the kingdom of God

chapters.n: Some of them used to live that way — but Christ changed them. They were washed in baptism, made holy, and declared right with God through Christ and the Spirit. Change is possible.

f.g: Declared righteous, put right with God.

chapters.n: Paul quotes a Corinthian slogan, “All things are lawful,” and qualifies it: not everything is helpful, and he won’t be enslaved by anything. JST: “All these things are not lawful unto me.”

f.g: Beneficial, helpful, wise.

f.w: brought under the power of any
f.g: Mastered or enslaved by any habit.

chapters.n: Some argued that bodily appetites, like eating, are merely natural. Paul answers that the body isn’t designed for sexual immorality — it is for the Lord, and the Lord cares for the body.

f.g: Food for the stomach — probably another Corinthian slogan.

chapters.n: The body matters eternally: God raised Jesus’ body, and He will raise ours by the same power.
Our bodies are members of Christ’s body. How could we join Christ’s members to a prostitute? Absolutely not!

f.g: Greek mē genoito — “May it never be!”

chapters.n: Sexual union creates a deep bond. Paul quotes Genesis — “two shall be one flesh” — showing that sex is never merely physical.

f.w: two, saith he, shall be one flesh

chapters.n: The person united to the Lord becomes one with Him in spirit — a far higher union.
Run from sexual sin. Unlike other sins, it is a sin against one’s own body, which was meant to be sacred.
Each person’s body is a temple where the Holy Ghost dwells. We don’t belong to ourselves.

f.w: your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Christ paid the price of our redemption with His own blood. So we honor God in how we use our bodies and spirits.

Paul now answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” was likely their own slogan favoring celibacy; the JST frames it as their saying, which Paul goes on to qualify.

f.w: the things whereof ye wrote unto me
f.g: The Corinthians had written Paul with questions; chapters 7–16 respond to them.
A polite way of saying to abstain from sexual relations.

chapters.n: Because sexual temptation was everywhere in Corinth, each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband. Marriage is the proper place for physical intimacy.

f.w: let every man have his own wife

chapters.n: Husband and wife owe each other affection and physical intimacy. The obligation runs equally both ways.

f.g: The kindness and marital intimacy that is owed to a spouse.

chapters.n: In marriage, neither spouse has sole say over his or her own body; each belongs to the other. Paul’s equal treatment of husband and wife was striking in his culture.

f.w: hath not power of her own body
f.g: Does not have exclusive authority over it.

chapters.n: Couples shouldn’t deprive each other, except by mutual agreement for a short time of focused fasting and prayer. Then they should come back together so Satan can’t exploit a lack of self-control.

f.g: Don’t withhold or deprive.
Lack of self-control.

chapters.n: Paul says this as a concession or allowance, not as a command.

f.g: As a concession, an allowance.

chapters.n: Paul wishes others could live as he does (apparently unmarried at the time), but recognizes each person has a different gift from God.
To the unmarried and widows, Paul says it is good to remain as he is — given the circumstances he will describe.

f.g: Some think Paul had been married earlier and was now a widower; scripture doesn’t say.

chapters.n: But if they can’t control their desires, they should marry. It is better to marry than to be consumed with passion.

f.g: Exercise self-control.
Burn with passion.

chapters.n: To married couples, Paul passes on the Lord’s own teaching: a wife should not separate from her husband.
If she does separate, she should remain unmarried or reconcile. And a husband should not divorce his wife.

f.g: Divorce.

chapters.n: For situations Jesus didn’t directly address, Paul gives his own apostolic counsel: a believing man married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay should not divorce her.

f.g: Not a quotation of Jesus’ earthly teaching, but Paul’s inspired counsel.

chapters.n: Likewise, a believing woman married to an unbelieving husband who wants to stay should not leave him.

f.g: Is not a Christian.

chapters.n: The believing spouse brings a holy influence into the home. The marriage isn’t defiled, and the children are under a sanctifying influence. A note in D&C 74 explains a related tradition about children and the law of Moses.

f.g: Set within the sphere of holy influence.

chapters.n: If the unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, let them go. The believer isn’t bound in such a case. God wants His people to live in peace.

f.g: Not enslaved or bound.

chapters.n: Who knows? By staying, a believing spouse might bring the other to Christ.
General principle: each person should live faithfully in whatever situation he was in when God called him. Paul teaches this in all the churches.

f.g: So let him live.

chapters.n: A Jewish convert shouldn’t try to hide his circumcision, and a Gentile convert shouldn’t get circumcised. Ethnic markers don’t determine standing with God.
Circumcision or not makes no difference. What matters is keeping God’s commandments.

f.w: keeping of the commandments of God

chapters.n: Each person should remain in the life situation he was in when he was called to Christ.

f.g: Here, one’s situation in life at conversion.

chapters.n: If you were a slave when converted, don’t let it trouble you — though if you can gain your freedom, take it.

f.g: Greek doulos — a slave or bond-servant. Many early Christians were slaves.

chapters.n: A slave who follows Christ is spiritually free in the Lord, while a free person who follows Christ becomes His servant. In Christ, worldly rank is turned upside down.
Christ bought you at the price of His own life. Don’t become enslaved to human opinions and masters.

f.w: Ye are bought with a price

chapters.n: Whatever your situation, remain in it with God. Faithfulness matters more than circumstances.

f.g: Stay close to God in that situation.

chapters.n: Regarding those who have never married, Paul has no direct command from the Lord, but offers his trustworthy judgment as one who received the Lord’s mercy.

f.g: Unmarried young people, especially young women of marriageable age.

chapters.n: Because of a “present distress” — perhaps persecution, famine, or the urgency of missionary work — Paul thinks it is wise to stay as one is for now.

f.g: A time of pressing difficulty in Paul’s day; the exact crisis is unknown.

chapters.n: If married, don’t seek to end it. If unmarried, don’t rush to marry during this crisis.

f.g: Free from (unmarried or released).

chapters.n: Still, marrying is not a sin. Paul only wants to spare them the added hardships married people would face in difficult times.

f.g: Practical worldly hardship.

chapters.n: Time is short. The JST shows Paul is speaking here to those called to the ministry: even married missionaries must give themselves fully to the Lord’s work while serving.

f.g: JST adds: “But I speak unto you who are called unto the ministry.”

chapters.n: Don’t let grief, joy, or possessions dominate you. Hold earthly things loosely.
Use the world without being consumed by it, because its present form is passing away.

f.w: the fashion of this world passeth away

f.g: Using it to the full, over-using.

chapters.n: Paul wants them free from anxieties. An unmarried servant can focus wholly on pleasing the Lord.

f.g: Anxiety, worry.

chapters.n: A married person must also attend to everyday responsibilities and to pleasing a spouse — a legitimate but divided focus.

f.w: how he may please his wife

chapters.n: The same is true for women: an unmarried woman can focus fully on holiness and the Lord, while a married woman must also care for her husband and home.

f.w: holy both in body and in spirit

chapters.n: Paul isn’t trying to trap or burden them, but to help them serve the Lord with undivided devotion.

f.g: A noose or trap — here, a restriction.
Proper, fitting.

chapters.n: If a man feels he isn’t treating his fiancée (or daughter) properly by delaying marriage, and she is getting older, they should marry. It is no sin.

f.w: pass the flower of her age
f.g: Beyond the usual age for marriage.
Interpreted either as his betrothed or as his unmarried daughter.

chapters.n: But one who is settled in his decision, under no pressure, and resolves not to marry does well too.

f.w: hath power over his own will
f.g: Has self-control and freedom to choose.

chapters.n: Both choices are good, but in the current crisis Paul judges the single path better. The JST reads this as a man who “giveth himself” in marriage.

f.g: In context of the present distress and full-time service, not as a general rule for all ages.

chapters.n: A wife is bound to her husband while he lives. If he dies, she may remarry — but only to a believer.

f.g: To a fellow believer.

f.w: as long as her husband liveth

chapters.n: Paul thinks a widow is happier remaining single, in his judgment — and he believes he has the Spirit of God in saying so.

f.w: I have the Spirit of God
f.g: Paul gently claims inspiration for his counsel.

chapters.n: Another question: may Christians eat meat that had been sacrificed to pagan idols? Much of the meat sold in Corinth came from temple sacrifices. Paul begins: knowledge can make us proud, but love builds others up.

f.g: Meat from animals sacrificed in pagan temples, later eaten at temple feasts or sold in markets.

chapters.n: Anyone who thinks he knows it all hasn’t yet learned how knowledge should be held — humbly.
What matters most is not what we know, but whether we love God — and are known by Him.
Paul agrees with the “knowledgeable” members on a basic point: idols are not real gods. There is only one true God.
People call many beings “gods” and “lords,” in heaven and on earth.

f.g: Latter-day Saints have often cited this verse in discussing the plurality of exalted beings, while Paul’s main point here is about pagan deities.

chapters.n: But for Christians there is one God, the Father, the source of all things, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were created and through whom we live.

f.w: one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things

chapters.n: Not everyone grasps this yet. Some recent converts still feel the idol’s power when they eat such meat, and so their sensitive conscience is wounded.

f.g: The inner sense of right and wrong.
Stained, made unclean.

chapters.n: Food itself doesn’t bring us closer to God or push us away. Eating or abstaining doesn’t change our standing.

f.w: meat commendeth us not to God

chapters.n: But be careful that your freedom doesn’t cause a weaker member to stumble in their faith.
If a new member sees a knowledgeable believer eating in an idol’s temple, he may be encouraged to do the same — while still believing it is worship of the idol.

f.w: sit at meat in the idol's temple
f.g: Recline at a meal in a pagan temple dining hall — a common social event in Corinth.

chapters.n: So your knowledge could destroy a brother for whom Christ died. That is a heavy cost for exercising a “right.”
Wounding a fellow member’s fragile conscience is not just a social misstep — it is sinning against Christ Himself.
Paul’s conclusion: if eating meat would cause his brother to fall, he would never eat meat again. Love limits liberty.

f.g: Cause to stumble or sin.

chapters.n: Paul defends his authority with rapid-fire questions. He is a true apostle: he has seen the risen Lord, and the Corinthian church itself is proof of his work.

f.w: have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord?

f.g: Free to use his rights, like the right to be supported.

chapters.n: Others might doubt Paul, but the Corinthians can’t — their conversion is the official seal stamping his apostleship as genuine.

f.g: A stamp of authenticity, like a wax seal on a document.

chapters.n: To those who question his credentials, Paul now presents his defense.

f.g: Interrogate, cross-examine, as in a legal hearing.

chapters.n: Don’t apostles have the right to be fed and housed by those they serve?

f.g: Here, right or authority.

chapters.n: Don’t they have the right to bring a believing wife along on their travels, as Peter, the other apostles, and the Lord’s brothers did?

f.g: A believing wife (a “sister” in the faith).

chapters.n: Are Paul and Barnabas the only missionaries expected to support themselves with secular work?

f.g: Refrain from working for a living.

chapters.n: Paul uses everyday examples: soldiers are paid, vineyard planters eat grapes, shepherds drink milk from their flocks. Workers deserve to benefit from their work.

f.g: At his own expense.

chapters.n: This isn’t merely human reasoning — the law of Moses teaches the same thing.

f.g: The law of Moses in the first five books of the Old Testament.

chapters.n: Moses’ law said not to muzzle an ox while it treads out grain, so it could eat as it worked. Paul asks whether God’s concern was really only for oxen.

f.w: Thou shalt not muzzle the mouth of the ox

f.g: In the KJV, any grain, such as wheat or barley.

chapters.n: The principle applies to people: those who plow and thresh should be able to work in hope of sharing the harvest.

f.g: Beats or treads grain to separate kernels from husks.

chapters.n: If Paul planted spiritual blessings among them, is it too much to receive some material support in return?

f.g: Material, physical things like food and money.

chapters.n: Others received support from the Corinthians; Paul had even more right. Yet he refused it and endured hardship so nothing would get in the gospel’s way.

f.g: Put up with everything.

chapters.n: Priests in the temple lived from the offerings brought there. Those who served at the altar received a share of the sacrifices.
Likewise, the Lord directed that full-time preachers of the gospel be supported by it.

f.w: they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel

chapters.n: But Paul has not used this right and isn’t hinting for it now. He would rather die than lose the privilege of preaching without pay.

f.g: His grounds for honest pride — preaching free of charge.

chapters.n: Preaching itself isn’t something to boast about — Paul is under divine compulsion to do it. He would be miserable if he didn’t.

f.w: woe is unto me, if I preach not the gospel

chapters.n: If he preached by his own choice, he could expect pay. But he was commissioned — entrusted with a stewardship — so preaching is simply his duty.

f.g: Here, a stewardship or commission entrusted to him.

chapters.n: His “reward” is the satisfaction of offering the gospel free of charge, not exploiting his rights.
Though free from obligation to anyone, Paul made himself everyone’s servant to win as many as possible to Christ.
Among Jews, Paul respected Jewish customs so he could reach them — for example, by having Timothy circumcised.
Among Gentiles who didn’t keep Moses’ law, he set aside those customs — though he was always under Christ’s law.
He came alongside the spiritually fragile, too. Paul adapted his approach to every audience, without compromising the gospel, to save some.

f.g: Adapting methods, not changing doctrine.

chapters.n: Paul does all this for the gospel’s sake, so that he can share in its blessings with them.

f.g: A sharer in the gospel’s blessings.

chapters.n: Corinth hosted the famous Isthmian Games. Paul says: in a race only one wins the prize, so run to win.

f.w: So run, that ye may obtain

chapters.n: Athletes in training exercise strict self-discipline to win a wreath that withers. Christians train for a crown that never fades.

f.g: Victors at the Isthmian Games received a wreath of pine or celery that soon withered.
Self-controlled.

chapters.n: Paul runs with a clear goal and boxes with purpose — not shadowboxing or swinging wildly at air.

f.g: Punching at nothing, wasted effort.

chapters.n: He disciplines his body and keeps it under control so that, after preaching to others, he himself won’t be disqualified.

f.g: Literally “give a black eye to” — strict self-discipline.
Disqualified, rejected after testing.

chapters.n: Paul draws a warning from Israel’s exodus. All the ancient Israelites were guided by the cloud of God’s presence and passed through the Red Sea.
Paul sees their passage through the sea and under the cloud as a kind of baptism, uniting them with Moses as their leader.

f.g: A symbolic baptism of water and cloud, foreshadowing Christian baptism.

chapters.n: They all ate manna — food from heaven that pointed to spiritual nourishment.
They all drank water from the rock in the wilderness. Paul says the true source was Christ — the premortal Jehovah — who accompanied and sustained Israel.
Even so, most of that generation displeased God and died in the wilderness. Great blessings didn’t guarantee faithfulness.
Their stories are warnings for us, so we won’t crave evil things as they did.
Don’t be idolaters like those who worshiped the golden calf with feasting and wild revelry.

f.w: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play

f.g: Here, idolatrous revelry, likely with immorality.

chapters.n: Don’t commit sexual sin as some Israelites did with the Moabites, when a plague killed thousands in a single day.

f.g: Numbers gives 24,000 total; Paul may be counting those who died in one day.

chapters.n: Don’t test the Lord as they did when they complained against Him and were bitten by fiery serpents. Paul identifies the Lord they tested as Christ.
Don’t grumble against God, as the Israelites did when many perished.

f.g: The destroying angel sent in judgment.

chapters.n: These events were recorded as examples to warn us — who live in the final era of history.

f.g: Examples, patterns, types.
The culmination of the ages, inaugurated by Christ.

chapters.n: So anyone who feels spiritually secure should be careful not to fall. Overconfidence is dangerous.
A promise of hope: your temptations are not unique. God is faithful and won’t let you be tempted beyond what you can bear; He will always provide a way out.

f.g: Typical of human experience.

chapters.n: Therefore, dear friends, run from idolatry — including participating in pagan temple feasts.
Paul appeals to their good sense: think it through for yourselves.

f.g: Weigh my words.

chapters.n: The sacrament cup and bread give us a real sharing in Christ’s blood and body. Eating sacred meals creates sacred bonds.

f.g: A Jewish term for the cup of wine blessed at the Passover meal.
Greek koinonia — participation, sharing.

chapters.n: Because we all share one loaf, we become one body — united in Christ.
Look at Israel: those who ate from the temple sacrifices shared in the altar and its worship.

f.g: The historical nation of Israel.

chapters.n: Is Paul saying the idol is real or that the meat itself is changed? No.
But behind pagan sacrifice are demonic forces, and Paul doesn’t want the saints sharing fellowship with them.
You can’t drink the Lord’s sacramental cup and also take part in idol feasts. Divided loyalty is impossible.
Do we want to provoke the Lord’s jealousy, as Israel did? We are not stronger than He is.
Repeating the Corinthian slogan, Paul adds: not everything helps, and not everything builds others up.

f.g: Build up, strengthen.

chapters.n: Don’t only look out for yourself — seek the good of others.

f.g: Old English sense: well-being, welfare.

chapters.n: Practical counsel: you may eat whatever is sold in the meat market without quizzing the seller about where it came from.

f.g: Meat market.

chapters.n: Paul quotes a psalm: all the earth and its produce belong to God, so food itself is a gift from Him.
If an unbeliever invites you to dinner and you choose to go, eat what is served without raising questions.

f.g: Invites you to a meal.

chapters.n: But if someone points out that the food was offered to idols, don’t eat it — for the sake of that person’s conscience.

f.w: for his sake that shewed it
f.g: Out of consideration for the one who told you.

chapters.n: Paul clarifies: it is the other person’s conscience he means. Your freedom isn’t ruled by another’s conscience, but you lovingly limit it for their sake.
If I eat with thanksgiving, why should I be condemned? Yet Paul still chooses love over insisting on his rights.

f.g: With thankfulness.

chapters.n: The great principle: whatever you do — eating, drinking, anything — do it all to bring glory to God.

f.w: do all to the glory of God

chapters.n: Don’t be a stumbling block to anyone — Jews, Gentiles, or fellow Church members.
Paul tries to accommodate everyone, seeking their good rather than his own, so that many may be saved.
This verse closes the previous discussion: follow Paul’s example of putting others first, just as he follows Christ’s example.

f.g: Greek mimetai — imitators.

chapters.n: Paul commends the saints for remembering him and holding to the teachings and practices he passed on to them.

f.g: Here, traditions or teachings handed down.

chapters.n: Paul sets out an order of headship: Christ is head of man, man of woman, and God the Father of Christ. Even Christ, though divine, honors His Father’s authority.

f.w: the head of Christ is God

f.g: Can mean authority, source, or the one who represents another.

chapters.n: In Corinth’s culture, a man praying or prophesying in worship with his head covered brought shame on his head — and on Christ.

f.g: Speaking by inspiration to others.

chapters.n: A woman praying or prophesying uncovered would shame her head. In that culture, a woman uncovered in public could look as disgraceful as one whose head was shaved. Note that women did pray and prophesy in worship.

f.w: all one as if she were shaven
f.g: Equally shameful as a shaved head, which was a sign of disgrace in that society.

chapters.n: Paul argues: if a woman won’t cover her head, she might as well cut her hair off. Since that would be shameful, she should be covered.

f.g: Hair cut short.

chapters.n: Man reflects God’s image and glory; woman is the glory of man. Paul draws on the creation account to support the custom.

f.w: the image and glory of God

chapters.n: In the creation story, the woman was made from the man.
And she was created as a partner for the man.
So a woman should wear a sign of authority on her head, “because of the angels” — perhaps because angels attend worship. The exact meaning is uncertain.

f.g: A symbol of authority — perhaps her own authority to pray and prophesy.
The meaning is debated; possibly angels as witnesses of proper order in worship.

chapters.n: But in the Lord, man and woman are not independent of each other. Neither is complete without the other — a core truth of eternal marriage.

f.w: neither is the man without the woman

chapters.n: Just as the first woman came from man, every man since has been born of a woman. And all of it comes from God.
Judge for yourselves whether it is proper for a woman to pray publicly uncovered in that setting.

f.g: Proper, fitting.

chapters.n: Paul appeals to common sense of his culture: long hair on a man was seen as disgraceful.

f.g: The natural order, or common custom accepted as natural.

chapters.n: But long hair is a woman’s glory, given her as a natural covering.

f.g: Something wrapped around, like a veil or mantle.

chapters.n: If anyone wants to argue, Paul says the churches have no other practice. These were customs for that time and place.

f.g: Argumentative, quarrelsome.

chapters.n: Now Paul gives no praise: their worship gatherings were doing more harm than good.

f.w: not for the better, but for the worse
f.g: Their meetings were making things worse.

chapters.n: He hears that when they meet as a congregation, they split into factions — and he partly believes it.
Divisions do serve one purpose: they reveal who is genuinely faithful.

f.g: Here, factions or parties, not necessarily false doctrine.
Tested and proven genuine.

chapters.n: Early Christians ate a shared meal with the sacrament. But the way the Corinthians did it, it was no longer truly the Lord’s Supper.

f.g: The sacrament, often celebrated as part of a shared meal (later called the love feast).

chapters.n: Wealthier members ate their own food first, while poorer members — who arrived after work — went hungry. Some even got drunk.

f.w: one is hungry, and another is drunken
f.g: A painful picture of class divisions at a sacred meal.

chapters.n: If you just want a meal, eat at home! Paul asks whether they despise God’s Church and humiliate the poor. He certainly cannot praise this.
Paul passes on what he received from the Lord: the night Jesus was betrayed, He took bread. This is one of the earliest written accounts of the Last Supper.

f.w: the same night in which he was betrayed

chapters.n: Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and said it was His body broken for them, to be eaten in remembrance of Him. Remembering Him is the heart of the sacrament.
After supper He took the cup, calling it the new covenant in His blood, and asked them to drink it in remembrance of Him.

f.g: New covenant.

chapters.n: Each time we take the sacrament, we proclaim Christ’s death and look forward to His return.
So anyone who takes the sacrament in an unworthy, careless way sins against the Lord’s body and blood.

f.g: In an unworthy manner — irreverently, or without repenting.

chapters.n: Each person should examine himself before partaking — reflecting honestly and repenting.
Those who partake carelessly, not recognizing the sacred meaning of the Lord’s body — including His body, the Church — bring judgment on themselves.

f.g: Here, judgment or condemnation.
Recognizing, distinguishing.

chapters.n: Paul links this to the illness and even deaths among them.

f.g: A gentle way of saying die.

chapters.n: If we honestly judged ourselves, we wouldn’t need to come under God’s judgment.
Even when the Lord disciplines us, it is loving correction to keep us from being condemned with the world.
So when you meet to eat together, wait for each other.

f.g: Wait so all can share together.

chapters.n: If you’re hungry, eat at home, so your gatherings don’t bring judgment on you. Paul will address other matters in person.

f.g: Arrange, regulate.

chapters.n: Paul turns to another question from their letter: spiritual gifts. He wants them to understand these properly.
Before conversion, they were swept along in the worship of lifeless idols that couldn’t speak — sometimes in emotional frenzy.

f.g: Speechless idols.

chapters.n: Here’s the test: no one speaking by God’s Spirit curses Jesus, and no one can truly confess Jesus as Lord except by the Holy Ghost.

f.g: Greek anathema — under a curse.

chapters.n: There are many kinds of gifts, but one Spirit gives them all.
There are different kinds of service, but the same Lord directs them.

f.g: Ministries, ways of serving.

chapters.n: There are different ways God works, but the same God works through them all. Spirit, Lord, and God — Paul mentions all three members of the Godhead.

f.g: Workings, activities.

chapters.n: Each person receives some manifestation of the Spirit — for the benefit of everyone, not just for personal display.

f.g: For the common good.

chapters.n: One receives the gift to speak with wisdom, another to speak with knowledge — both by the same Spirit.

f.g: Here, inspired wise counsel — not the Latter-day Saint health code (D&C 89), which shares the name.

chapters.n: Another receives exceptional faith; another gifts of healing.
Others receive the gifts of miracles, prophecy, discerning spirits, speaking in tongues, and interpreting tongues.

f.g: Various languages — inspired speech in a language unknown to the speaker.

chapters.n: All these come from the same Spirit, who distributes them to each person as He chooses.
Paul compares the Church to a human body: many parts, one body. So it is with Christ’s body.
Through one Spirit all were baptized into one body — Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free — and all drink from that same Spirit.
A body isn’t one part — it is many.

f.g: Diversity is built into the design.

chapters.n: If a foot said, “I’m not a hand, so I don’t belong,” it would still be part of the body. Feeling less important doesn’t make you less needed.

f.w: I am not of the body
f.g: Paul speaks to members who feel their gifts don’t count.

chapters.n: Same with an ear that wishes it were an eye — it still belongs.

f.g: A body part that seems less noticeable than the eye.

chapters.n: If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, how would it smell? Every function matters.

f.g: The body would lose essential abilities.

chapters.n: God Himself has placed each part in the body exactly as He chose.
If everyone were the same part, there would be no body at all.

f.g: Uniformity would destroy the body.

chapters.n: So there are many parts, yet one body.
Now Paul speaks to those who feel superior: the eye can’t say it doesn’t need the hand, nor the head the feet.

f.w: I have no need of thee
f.g: The attitude of proud members toward others.

chapters.n: In fact, the parts that seem weakest are indispensable.

f.g: Like internal organs — hidden but vital.

chapters.n: We give special care and covering to parts we consider less presentable.

f.g: Less presentable parts, which we modestly clothe.

chapters.n: Our presentable parts need no special treatment. God arranged the body to give more honor to the parts that lacked it.

f.g: Blended, mixed together harmoniously.

chapters.n: So there would be no division in the body, but all parts would care for one another equally.

f.g: Split, division.

chapters.n: When one part hurts, the whole body hurts. When one part is honored, all rejoice.

f.w: all the members suffer with it

chapters.n: The Corinthian saints are Christ’s body, and each is an individual part of it.
God placed in the Church apostles first, then prophets, then teachers, followed by other gifts and roles. Latter-day Saints see this order restored in the Church today.

f.g: Helpers and administrators or guides.

chapters.n: Are all apostles or prophets or teachers or miracle workers? Obviously not.

f.g: The questions in Greek expect the answer “no.”

chapters.n: Not all heal, speak in tongues, or interpret. The Corinthians overvalued tongues; Paul shows it is only one gift among many.
Seek earnestly the greater gifts. But Paul is about to show them something even more excellent: charity.

Paul’s famous chapter on love. Even if he could speak every human and angelic language, without charity he would be just noise — like a clanging gong. The Corinthians prized tongues; Paul says love matters more.

f.g: Greek agape — selfless, Christlike love; the KJV renders it “charity.”
A noisy bronze gong or instrument — loud but empty.

chapters.n: Prophecy, deep understanding, all knowledge, and even mountain-moving faith amount to nothing without love.
Giving everything to the poor, or even dying as a martyr, gains nothing if done without love. Motive matters.

f.w: bestow all my goods to feed the poor
give my body to be burned
f.g: Some ancient manuscripts read “that I may boast.”

chapters.n: Paul describes love in action: it is patient and kind; it doesn’t envy, brag, or swell with pride. Mormon’s parallel description in the Book of Mormon closely matches these words.

f.g: Doesn’t show off or boast.

chapters.n: Love isn’t rude or self-seeking, isn’t quickly angered, and doesn’t keep a record of wrongs or assume the worst.

f.g: Rudely, indecently.
Doesn’t plot harm or keep score of wrongs.

chapters.n: Love takes no pleasure in wrongdoing but rejoices whenever truth wins.
Love bears up under anything, keeps trusting, keeps hoping, and endures to the end.

f.g: Literally “covers” or protects; puts up with all.

chapters.n: Love never fails or ends. Prophecies, tongues, and present knowledge are temporary tools that will one day be outgrown.
Right now our knowledge and our prophecies are partial and incomplete.

f.g: Partially, incompletely.

chapters.n: When perfection comes — at the Lord’s coming and our full redemption — what is partial will be replaced.

f.g: Complete, mature; the state of full knowledge in God’s presence.

chapters.n: Like growing up, we will one day leave our childish understanding behind.

f.g: Laid aside the ways of a child.

chapters.n: Now we see God’s truths dimly, like a blurry reflection in an ancient bronze mirror. Then we will see face to face and know as fully as God knows us.

f.g: In a mirror, indistinctly — ancient mirrors were polished metal with poor reflections.

chapters.n: Faith, hope, and charity remain — but the greatest is charity, the pure love of Christ.
Pursue love above all, and also seek spiritual gifts — especially prophecy, which blesses others directly.

f.g: Speak inspired messages that teach and testify, not only foretell.

chapters.n: A person speaking in a tongue no one understands talks to God, not to people. In the Spirit he speaks mysteries, but no one else benefits.

f.g: A language unknown to the hearers. (“Unknown” is added by the KJV translators.)

chapters.n: Prophecy speaks to people to build them up, encourage them, and comfort them.
Tongues build up only the speaker; prophecy builds up the whole congregation.
Paul values tongues, but prophecy is greater — unless the tongue is interpreted so the Church benefits.
If Paul came speaking only in tongues, what good would it do them? They need revelation, knowledge, prophecy, or teaching they can understand.

f.g: Something God makes known.

chapters.n: Even a flute or harp must play distinct notes, or no one can recognize the tune.

f.g: Clear differences between notes.

chapters.n: If a bugle gives an unclear signal, soldiers won’t know to prepare for battle.

f.g: A muddled, unclear signal.

chapters.n: Likewise, unless you speak words people understand, you’re just talking into the air.
There are many languages in the world, and every one carries meaning.

f.g: Meaning.

chapters.n: But if I don’t understand someone’s language, we are foreigners to each other.

f.g: Greek barbaros — a foreigner whose speech sounded like “bar-bar” to Greeks.

chapters.n: Since you’re eager for spiritual gifts, seek ones that strengthen the Church.

f.g: Literally “zealots for spirits.”

chapters.n: So whoever speaks in a tongue should pray for the gift to interpret.
When praying in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind gets nothing from it.

f.g: Unproductive; my mind isn’t engaged.

chapters.n: So Paul will pray and sing both with the Spirit and with understanding — heart and mind working together.
Otherwise, how can someone who doesn’t understand say “Amen” to your prayer of thanks? Saying Amen means agreeing with what was said.

f.g: Hebrew for “so be it” or “truly” — a congregation’s affirmation.
An outsider or inquirer unfamiliar with the gift.

chapters.n: Your prayer may be fine, but it doesn’t help anyone else.

f.g: Not built up.

chapters.n: Paul thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than any of them — so he isn’t criticizing the gift itself.

f.g: Perhaps including Paul’s ability to preach in many languages.

chapters.n: But in church he’d rather say five words people understand than ten thousand in a tongue.

f.g: Clear speech outweighs impressive display.

chapters.n: Grow up in your thinking. Be innocent as babies regarding evil, but mature in understanding.
Paul cites Isaiah: God warned Israel He would speak through foreign-speaking invaders, yet they still wouldn’t listen.

f.w: With men of other tongues and other lips

chapters.n: So tongues are a sign mainly to unbelievers, while prophecy blesses believers.
If outsiders walk in while everyone is speaking in tongues, they’ll think you’re out of your minds.

f.g: Insane, raving.

chapters.n: But if all are speaking inspired truth plainly, an unbeliever who comes in will feel convicted and examined by what he hears.

f.g: Convicted, persuaded of his sins.

chapters.n: The secrets of his heart will be exposed, and he will fall down and worship God, declaring that God is truly among them.

f.w: God is in you of a truth

chapters.n: What should worship look like? Each person brings something — a hymn, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, an interpretation. Everything should build up others.

f.g: A hymn or song of praise.

f.w: Let all things be done unto edifying

chapters.n: If people speak in tongues, limit it to two or three, one at a time, with someone interpreting.

f.g: In turn, one after another.

chapters.n: If there is no interpreter, the speaker should stay silent in the meeting and speak privately to God.

f.g: Don’t speak aloud in the meeting.

chapters.n: Let two or three prophets speak, and let others weigh what is said.

f.g: Let the others evaluate it.

chapters.n: If someone seated receives a revelation, the first speaker should yield.

f.g: Be quiet.

chapters.n: All can prophesy in turn so everyone learns and is encouraged.
Prophets remain in control of their spiritual gifts; true inspiration doesn’t force a person into uncontrolled behavior.

f.g: Under the speaker’s control.

chapters.n: God is not a God of chaos but of peace — that is the pattern in all congregations.

f.w: God is not the author of confusion

chapters.n: Paul addresses a specific disorder involving women speaking in meetings. The JST changes “speak” to “rule,” suggesting the issue was authority over the meeting, not women’s participation — which Paul assumes elsewhere (11:5).

f.w: it is not permitted unto them to speak
f.g: JST reads “to rule.”

chapters.n: Disruptive questions should be saved for discussion at home. Paul is addressing a local problem of order in that culture; the JST again reads “rule” for “speak.”

f.g: A remedy for disruptive questioning during worship.

chapters.n: Did God’s word originate with the Corinthians? Are they the only ones who received it? They should follow the practice of the wider Church.

f.g: A rebuke of Corinthian independence.

chapters.n: Anyone who claims to be a prophet or spiritual should recognize that Paul’s instructions are the Lord’s commandments.
Whoever refuses to recognize this will not be recognized either.

f.g: Some manuscripts read “he is not recognized.”

chapters.n: So, brothers and sisters, eagerly seek prophecy, and don’t forbid speaking in tongues.
Do everything in a fitting and orderly way.
Paul begins his great chapter on the Resurrection by reminding the saints of the gospel he first preached — the gospel they accepted and on which they now stand.

f.w: the gospel which I preached unto you

chapters.n: This gospel saves them if they hold firmly to it — otherwise their belief would have been for nothing.

f.g: Hold fast to, keep firmly.
Believed without purpose or result.

chapters.n: The heart of the message, which Paul himself received: Christ died for our sins, as the scriptures foretold.

f.g: Handed on — a term for passing down sacred tradition.

chapters.n: He was buried, and He rose again on the third day, just as scripture said.
Paul lists eyewitnesses: the risen Christ appeared to Peter, then to the Twelve.
He appeared to more than five hundred believers at once. Most were still alive and could be asked — a bold invitation to check the facts.

f.w: above five hundred brethren at once
f.g: This appearance is mentioned only here.
Died.

chapters.n: Then He appeared to James, the Lord’s brother, and to all the apostles.

f.g: Likely James the Lord’s brother, later a leader in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Last of all He appeared to Paul, who calls himself like a child born at the wrong time — an apostle called unusually late.

f.g: An untimely birth — a vivid image of his sudden, irregular calling.

chapters.n: Paul sees himself as the least of the apostles, unworthy of the title, because he once persecuted the Church.

f.w: I persecuted the church of God

f.g: Fit, worthy.

chapters.n: Yet God’s grace made him who he is, and it wasn’t wasted: Paul worked harder than anyone — though he credits God’s grace for it.

f.w: by the grace of God I am what I am

chapters.n: Whether Paul or the other apostles preached, the message was the same, and the Corinthians believed it.

f.g: The apostles taught a united witness.

chapters.n: If the risen Christ is preached, how can some Corinthians claim the dead don’t rise? Greek thinking often regarded the body as a prison to escape, not something to restore.
If there is no resurrection at all, then Christ Himself didn’t rise.

f.g: Paul follows the denial to its logical end.

chapters.n: And if Christ didn’t rise, all preaching and all faith are empty.

f.g: Empty, worthless.

chapters.n: The apostles would then be lying about God, falsely testifying that He raised Christ.
Paul repeats the point: deny resurrection in general and you deny Christ’s.

f.g: The two stand or fall together.

chapters.n: If Christ isn’t raised, their faith is useless and they remain unforgiven. The Resurrection confirms that His Atonement worked.

f.w: ye are yet in your sins

chapters.n: And believers who died would simply be lost forever.
If our hope in Christ were only for this life, we would be the most pitiable people of all.
But Christ truly has risen! He is the firstfruits — the first portion of a harvest that guarantees the rest will follow.

f.g: The first sheaf of harvest offered to God, promising the full harvest.

chapters.n: Death came into the world through a man; resurrection comes through a man too.
Because of Adam, all die; because of Christ, all will be made alive again. The Resurrection is a universal gift.

f.w: in Christ shall all be made alive

chapters.n: There is an order: Christ first, then at His coming those who belong to Him, and others later.

f.w: every man in his own order

chapters.n: Then comes the end, when Christ, having conquered every opposing power, presents the kingdom to the Father.

f.w: delivered up the kingdom to God

chapters.n: Christ must reign until all enemies are under His feet, as the psalm foretold.

f.w: till he hath put all enemies under his feet

chapters.n: The final enemy Christ will destroy is death itself.
Quoting a psalm that God put all things under the Son’s feet, Paul notes that the Father who did this is of course not included.

f.w: he hath put all things under his feet

chapters.n: When all is subdued, the Son Himself will remain subject to the Father, so God will be all in all. Father and Son are distinct, perfectly united beings.

f.g: Supreme over everything.

f.w: the Son also himself be subject

chapters.n: Paul points to a practice the Corinthians knew: baptism on behalf of the dead. It would make no sense if the dead never rise. Latter-day Saints perform this ordinance in temples today.
Why would the apostles risk danger every hour if there were no resurrection?

f.g: Danger.

chapters.n: Paul swears by his pride in them: he faces death every day.

f.g: I face mortal danger constantly.

chapters.n: If he fought “beasts” at Ephesus — probably fierce human opponents — for no eternal purpose, he might as well live for pleasure. Paul quotes the hopeless motto of Isaiah’s day.

f.w: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die

f.g: Likely figurative for violent opposition.

chapters.n: Don’t be fooled: bad company ruins good character. Paul quotes a well-known Greek saying.

f.g: A line from the Greek poet Menander: bad company corrupts good morals.

chapters.n: Wake up to what is right and stop sinning. Some among them don’t truly know God — and that should shame them.
Paul anticipates a question: how are the dead raised? What kind of body will they have?
Look at a seed: it must be buried and “die” before new life springs up.

f.g: Made alive.

chapters.n: You plant a bare kernel, not the full plant that will grow.

f.g: A naked seed.

chapters.n: God gives each seed the body He designed for it. The resurrected body is connected to the mortal one but far more glorious.

f.w: to every seed his own body

chapters.n: There are many kinds of bodies — humans, animals, fish, birds — each different.

f.w: All flesh is not the same flesh
f.g: God’s creation shows great variety.

chapters.n: There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies with different glories. The JST adds “bodies telestial,” matching the three degrees of glory revealed to Joseph Smith in D&C 76.

f.g: JST adds “and bodies telestial.”

chapters.n: The sun, moon, and stars each shine with a different glory. Paul uses this to illustrate differing glories in the resurrection.

f.w: one star differeth from another star in glory

chapters.n: So with the resurrection: the body is buried subject to decay; it is raised never to decay again.

f.g: Buried in a body that decays.

chapters.n: Buried in humiliation and weakness, it is raised in glory and power.
It is buried a natural body and raised a spiritual body — still physical, but now governed by the spirit and immortal.

f.g: A body of flesh and bone quickened by spirit rather than blood.

chapters.n: Genesis says the first man, Adam, became a living soul. Christ, the “last Adam,” became a life-giving spirit who raises all.

f.w: The first man Adam was made a living soul

f.g: Life-giving.

chapters.n: The natural body comes first, and the spiritual (resurrected) body comes afterward.

f.g: Mortality precedes resurrection.

chapters.n: Adam was made from the earth; Christ is the Lord from heaven.
Mortals share Adam’s earthly nature; those who follow Christ will share His heavenly nature.
Just as we have borne Adam’s image, we will bear the image of the resurrected Christ.

f.w: bear the image of the heavenly

chapters.n: Mortal flesh and blood, in its corruptible state, can’t inherit God’s kingdom; it must be changed.

f.w: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God
f.g: Resurrected bodies are flesh and bone, not mortal flesh and blood.

chapters.n: Paul reveals a mystery: not everyone will die, but everyone will be transformed.
In an instant, at the final trumpet, the dead will rise imperishable and the living will be changed.
This decaying, mortal body must be clothed with incorruption and immortality.

f.w: this mortal must put on immortality

chapters.n: Then Isaiah’s prophecy will be fulfilled: death is swallowed up in victory.

f.w: Death is swallowed up in victory

chapters.n: Paul taunts death in Hosea’s words: Where is your sting? Where is your victory?

f.w: O death, where is thy sting?

chapters.n: Death’s sting is sin, and sin draws its power from the law, which exposes and condemns it.

f.w: the strength of sin is the law

chapters.n: But thanks be to God, who gives us victory over sin and death through Jesus Christ!
So stand firm and immovable, always giving yourselves fully to the Lord’s work, knowing that nothing you do for Him is wasted.
Paul turns to practical business: a collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem, which he had also organized among the churches in Galatia.
Each Sunday, every member should set aside an amount based on how God had blessed them, so no last-minute collection would be needed. Christians were already gathering on the first day of the week.

f.w: the first day of the week
f.g: Sunday, the day of Christ’s resurrection.
In proportion to income.

chapters.n: When Paul arrives, he’ll send trusted representatives they choose, with letters of introduction, to carry their gift to Jerusalem. Accountability protected everyone.

f.g: Generous gift.

chapters.n: If it seems wise for Paul to go too, the delegates will travel with him.

f.g: Fitting, appropriate.

chapters.n: Paul plans to visit after traveling through Macedonia (northern Greece).

f.g: The northern Greek region including Philippi and Thessalonica.

chapters.n: He might stay with them through the winter, when sea travel was dangerous, so they can help send him on his next journey.

f.g: Ships rarely sailed the Mediterranean in winter.
Provide supplies and help for travel.

chapters.n: He doesn’t want a quick passing visit, but hopes to stay a while, if the Lord allows.
Meanwhile he will stay in Ephesus — where he is writing — until Pentecost, the spring harvest festival.

f.g: A Jewish feast fifty days after Passover.

chapters.n: A wide, productive door for missionary work has opened in Ephesus — along with many opponents.
If Timothy comes, make sure he feels at ease among you; he does the Lord’s work just as Paul does.

f.g: Timothy was young and perhaps timid.

chapters.n: Don’t look down on him. Send him back to Paul in peace; Paul is expecting him with the other brethren.

f.g: Look down on, treat with contempt.

chapters.n: Paul urged Apollos to visit Corinth, but Apollos decided now wasn’t the time. He would come later. Paul shows no rivalry with him.
A string of short commands: be alert, stand firm in faith, be courageous, be strong.

f.g: Act with courage and maturity.

chapters.n: And do everything with love — the theme of chapter 13 in a single line.
The household of Stephanas were among the first converts in Achaia and devoted themselves to serving the saints.

f.g: Among the first converts in the Roman province of southern Greece.
Devoted themselves (no negative sense).

chapters.n: Paul asks the Corinthians to follow and support such devoted servants and fellow workers.
Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus had visited Paul, likely carrying the Corinthians’ letter, and made up for the Corinthians’ absence.

f.w: that which was lacking on your part
f.g: Your absence — they brought a bit of Corinth to Paul.

chapters.n: They encouraged Paul and the saints alike. Paul urges the Church to recognize such people.
The congregations in the province of Asia send greetings, along with Aquila and Priscilla and the congregation meeting in their home.

f.g: The Roman province in western modern Turkey, capital Ephesus.

chapters.n: All the brethren send greetings. Greet each other with a holy kiss of affection.
Paul takes the pen from his scribe and writes this greeting in his own hand, authenticating the letter.
A solemn warning: anyone who doesn’t love the Lord is under a curse. Then an Aramaic prayer: “Our Lord, come!”

f.g: Greek — accursed, set apart for destruction.
Aramaic — “Our Lord, come!” or “Our Lord has come.”

chapters.n: Paul closes with his familiar blessing of the Lord’s grace.

f.w: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Despite the hard corrections in this letter, Paul ends with love for all of them in Christ.

f.w: My love be with you all
f.g: Only here does Paul end a letter with his own love.
